utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody, and welcome. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. All the accused are here. I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes, Mr. Josse and Ms. Condon. I take it that they are all working at the office, preparing for other witnesses. Correct. For the Prosecution, I notice Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Elderkin and Mr. Vanderpuye. As usual, the column is in the way. Yes, there was a leftover yesterday from -- in the wake of the submission from Madame Fauveau. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Elderkin has one exhibit from his witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay, I understand that. Yes, Mr. Elderkin, you can remain where you are if you have a microphone nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yesterday, we did not conclude the exhibit tendering process because we had little time left, and we required that for Ms. Fauveau's submission. Go ahead, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Just the one exhibit, which is the photograph that the witness marked. That was P2103 at page 212, and that's been numbered PIC107 with those annotations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Elderkin. Any objections? None. It is so admitted. The Defence barely cross-examined the witness, so I take it there are no Defence exhibits. Okay. So Mr. Elderkin, if you've got other work to do, you may leave. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As you know, from the time change I don't have perhaps the dates and times and numbers that I might. I'm giving you a general background --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By the way, before you continue, we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. The reason is today we shifted the sitting from the afternoon to the morning, with the result that this sitting clashed with the Haradinaj sitting, which is also in the morning, and Judge Stole, we came to an agreement that he sits there and we proceed pursuant to 15 bis ourselves. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can give you an outline from my memory and experience that will help, I think, respond in a general sense to Ms. Fauveau's remarks. In relation to the discovery and providing the Defence with documents relating to demography, we have worked for several years now with Ms. Radovanovic firstly with the Blagojevic case and secondly for this case, where we have set her up on her own computer in our building and gave her full access to all the material that our demographics people used in their reports, and we've responded to their questions whenever asked. And as far as I know, there are no questions or requests that went unanswered. And so they have had full access to all that material. And I have spoken to Mr. Zivanovic, and if he has material that he mentioned yesterday that they didn't use, we will make every effort to get that kind of material to them as well, though we have not been asked for that before. Specifically regarding the document that was brought up by -- I think first by Mr. Zivanovic, as you recall, I asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, it's 1D312.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd asked him where he'd gotten that. I had not seen this document before. And as you recall, he told us he got it from the RS Commission. We are looking in RS Commission records to see if we have it, though we have made our RS Commission records available to the Defence many, many months ago, and I believe if we had it, they would have been given it. This is not a document that we've ever translated or that I'm aware that anybody has set their eyes on. And it's a January 1994 document. The relevance, I think, was explained by the witness. It has some relevance; it's an interesting document. I do not think it's Rule 68. In fact, if anything, in my view, it's inculpatory. It gives the numbers, and I can't tell and I don't remember what was said yesterday, but it gives certain numbers of Muslims that came into the enclave, and as you know, it's our case that that is largely a result of the six strategic objectives, the directive force saying move the Muslim people out and those people came into the enclave, so I don't see how it is exculpatory, how it affects the credibility of any evidence. I think it's interesting, I think it's relevant. Had I seen it, I would have, we would have given it to the Defence. In particular, it came -- the collection that Ms. Fauveau was referring to, it came from a collection that we refer to as the cobblestone collection, the other version of it, that is, which is an unsigned, from what I gather, I've been able to see it on the computer, it's an unsigned version of the same stamped version that Mr. Zivanovic came up with. Now, and as we have told the Defence, we have had many communications with them about the cobblestone collection. They have full access to the cobblestone collection on EDS, EDS now with the updates that the OTP, the ICTY have done, I'm told that it's actually a better search engine than the Zy that the OTP has. But that collection, in particular, was a collection that was obtained by SFOR forces, and I believe it was 1988, 1989, I don't remember exactly, but when they searched an illegal weapons cache, they came up in the Zvornik area with a lot of documents as well. The US Army scanned those documents and then returned the originals. We have never seen the originals since, but the US Army gave us their scanned versions. It took us months and months to make any sense out of the electronic versions they gave us. It's still a collection that's very difficult to search. We have searched and searched and searched that collection, just pounded it with Cyrillic search-readers and others mainly for 1995, mainly for military-related documents, names, dates. Still, in the Blagojevic case, we -- the Blagojevic team found a document by General Mladic which has been used in this case in that collection that we had not been able to find, because I believe they may have just printed -- had gone over the documents individually. So the search engine is very bad in that, in that it would not have been an area -- a January '94 one-off civilian document that talks about estimates. Had I seen it, we would have kept it, but it's not something we specifically searched for, nor were we asked for, nor did we come across. Now that we have it, we're happy to have it, and I'm happy to -- if they have any other clues and any other thing they want us to help them search for, we will. We can now see the number on this document, and the US Army put numbers on it so we can now look at those ranges of documents that were scanned by the army at the same time to see if there's related documents, and we'll do that, but that's -- that's the basic background on the situation where we find ourselves with this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Do you wish to comment back, Madame Fauveau or Ms. Nikolic? Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I will limit myself just to the part that concerns the work of Ms. Radovanovic. Concerning the document, I suppose Ms. Fauveau will address the Chamber. I can say that Ms. Radovanovic had access to the documents of the Prosecution and worked with them for seven days, and we appreciate this cooperation. However, concerning the documents that Mrs. Radovanovic will use in her work, the Prosecution asked us to specify what we wanted to decide whether they can give us access to those documents, so what we found to be relevant in the expert report and what we thought could be useful, we asked for. So there was no blanket access of our expert to the Prosecution's material. But if she continues to have access to Prosecution material, I suppose that our request will be expanded. And as Mr. McCloskey said, I suppose that we will ask for more than we have at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm rather astonished by what I heard. First of all, of course, yes, we have access on the EDS to the general collection which contains I don't know how many millions of documents. We never received an index of documents that is in this infamous cobblestone collection. We can randomly find an interesting document or we can search for one document by document, and I don't know how many years that would take to the Defence team. I don't know how the Prosecutor can say that we have a search engine that is better than the Prosecution's. We have the same search engine, and we don't have the same resources as the Prosecutor. On another level concerning exculpatory and inculpatory material in that collection, I believe that this goes against this particular accused in the particular period concerning particular events. In 1992, there were people on all three sides who were expelled, so in our case, for every inculpatory document there is an exculpatory document in the collection. In this warrant arrest [as interpreted] for Blagojevic, the number of population in Srebrenica was mentioned just before the fall, and the only mention there is of 40.000 persons, and that results partially from the document that this Prosecutor had and that he never shared with the Blagojevic Defence during the Blagojevic case. I would like the same thing repeated in our case. That's why I would like the Prosecutor to share with us all the documents in his possession, all the documents that refer to the number of the population, and all the numbers related to humanitarian issues in the Srebrenica case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to be very straightforward. Are you asking for a remedy, apart from asking us to enjoin the Prosecution to make further searches and disclose whatever they come across, Madame Fauveau? Are you satisfied with that or are you asking for the pound of flesh, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I am happy with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need to respond further, Mr. McCloskey? May I just point out one thing in relation to this document. This document, in my mind, presents two facets. The first is what you referred to, namely, the classification of the three kinds of components of the population in Srebrenica in January of 1994, those who were the ordinary residents, and then a second classification and the third classification. One was 9.000 something, the other one was 10.000 something, and the other one was 16.000 something, a total of 37.000. But then there is another facet to it which goes to the Rule 68 business, namely, that there was a specific request by the person who sent that document to his superiors or to the office in Sarajevo, not to disclose or not to make that document available to foreign institutions, because with those foreign institutions, their presentation was there were 45.000 persons living in Srebrenica at the time, and this is January 1994. So for whatever that -- so for whatever weight that might carry, I think I will take advantage of what I have just said and proceed in line with the request of Madame Fauveau and enjoin you to make terra ^ 9:20:47 searches into whatever collection you may have in relation to the demography aspect of the case, and if there are any other documents that you come across that you were not aware of and maybe have not been put at the disposal of the Defence expert or the Defence teams, for that matter, that you do so. I'm sure you will. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, Mr. President, we're planning on it and we will get right on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just make a correction in the transcript. I think the Chamber understood me well. It's page 7, line 10. I spoke of the -- not of the warrant arrest but of the decision of the Appeals Chamber of the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I hadn't noticed that, but I had heard you say it. Thank you. So I think Mr. McCloskey will switch places with Mr. Vanderpuye, or vice versa. Do you wish -- one moment, I'll let Mr. Vanderpuye address himself. Mr. Vanderpuye, to you wish to address the Chamber before the witness comes in or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed, I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There are two issues. Good morning, everybody, and good morning to the Chamber. The first issue is relative to the witness's status, and I would ask if the Court would be inclined to give him a caution pursuant to Rule 90(E), I believe it is. The other issue is that during the course of proofing this witness, he had asked or requested protective measures, and I had forwarded an e-mail to the Defence basically outlining what had transpired, in our view, as to it. The witness had indicated that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ultimately, I don't know what the decision will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if the decision will be to proceed without protective measures. But what you are going to say now could -- I don't know. I mean, so let's go into private session and discuss this in private session. Then we hear the other side or we just hear you, I don't know, and we'll take a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning to you, Witness, and welcome once more to this Tribunal. Before I hand you over to Mr. Vanderpuye for his examination-in-chief, I wish to alert you to a right that you have under our rules as it relates to the testimony that you are about to give. You, according to the information that we have, lived part of the events that are the subject matter of this case, and although I have no idea what you are going to testify, it is my responsibility, as the Presiding Judge, to draw your attention to the following: I don't know if this will be the case, but you may be asked questions, either by the Prosecution or by any of the Defence teams, and in your mind you conclude that if you answer that question or those questions, you might be exposing yourself to criminal proceedings - I don't know if that will be the case or not, I don't know that it will be, but just in case you are asked such questions - then you may object to answering those questions if they tend to incriminate you. Now, it is not an absolute right. In other words, the position will be as follows: If you object, then we have to make an assessment. When I say "we," it's the three Judges up here, and we will consider your submission, we will consider other submissions, and we might decide to grant you exemption from answering those questions. But we may decide not to grant you exemption and to compel you to answer those questions. If we do, I want to put your mind at rest, that whatever you say in reply to those questions shall not be used as evidence against you in any subsequent proceedings, unless these proceedings are about false testimony, but I don't think we need to talk about that for the time being. Is this clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And has it been explained to you already before or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Prosecutor did say something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So feel free, if there are any such questions, to draw your attention if you wish to object. So I suggest now we go into private session for the first part of the direct, and then we can proceed in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I participated in the war from the very start until the end. I can't give you the exact date, but from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would that be in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you demobilised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was on the 6th of April, 2006 [sic].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following your mobilisation, can you tell -- well, tell us where you were assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean the wartime period?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My village, Pilica, had its own independent battalion until mid-1994, from the very beginning until mid-1994. So in 1994, I think that this battalion joined in with the neighbouring village of Lokanj, and from that time on they formed a single battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just clarify with you something that appears on the record, and that's at page 22, line 10 for my colleagues. In answer to the question when you were demobilised, the transcript reads: "That was the 6th of April, 2006." Is that correct or was that 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I may have made a mistake. It was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Until 1994, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war, in the very first few days when the war broke out, there was a meeting at a playground or a sports area, and then I was assigned by the police and the military representatives there to be the commander of a company, and I was the company commander for a very brief period of time, maybe one month. Quite soon, I got into conflict with the battalion command, and they dismissed me from that post. And until November 1994, I think, I was just a rank-and-file soldier on the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1994, with respect to your position, did your assignment or tasks change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said before that these two villages merged into one battalion, despite a certain tension that existed between those two villages. There was a previous attempt -- there had been a previous attempt to merge these two into one battalion, but it was unsuccessful. I think it was in November 1994 that I was appointed assistant battalion commander for intelligence and security. My rank was that of a private.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this position as assistant for intelligence and security, to whom were you subordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was directly subordinated to the battalion commander and his deputy. There was also an indirect chain through which we contacted with the assistant brigade commander for intelligence and security. We reported to him every 30th day of the month, and we received from him guidelines and instructions, for instance, what to pay special attention to in the following period and what to report about to the battalion commander so that battalion commander can take appropriate measures. So I was exclusively subordinated to the battalion commander and his deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1994, who was the battalion commander for the battalion you were assigned to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I should note that there were major staffing problems in many battalions, including mine, and many battalion commanders and deputy battalion commanders were soldiers, privates. My battalion commander was Milan Stanojevic. I'm not sure if he had a rank. Perhaps he didn't, but he was a brave, courageous soldier who was tested in the war, and he was greatly respected within the battalion and even further afield. His deputy was Momir Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time in 1994, who was the assistant chief of security for the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The assistant brigade commander for intelligence and security was Mr. Drago Nikolic, who then had the rank of lieutenant, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you recall, who was the chief of security for the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. There is no such post, chief of security. There was only one security organ, and it was led by Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have contact with Mr. Nikolic in the performance of your duties in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already said that. Every 30th day of the month, we had a briefing at which we reported to him about the situation in our unit, and I suppose he reported on to the brigade commander to enable the brigade commander to take tangible steps in the form of orders to battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you describe your professional relationship with Mr. Nikolic during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what would be noteworthy there. We had a decent relationship in terms of cooperation and the things we had to agree on. We were in contact a couple of times a month to exchange information. I really don't know what would be of interest there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any personal relationship with Mr. Nikolic during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't know each other at all. We had official contacts between brigade and battalion, and we talked of other things we needed to discuss.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just move on to July of 1995. Now, in July of 1995, did you occupy the same position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was your office situated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The battalion command was located in a house in Manojlovici village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many individuals were assigned to the command or did the command consist of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around ten; the commander, deputy commander, assistant commander for intelligence and security, assistant battalion commander for morale and information, a clerk for general affairs, two drivers, two messengers, and perhaps two other men who are operations officers or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've named a lot of people. Do you recall their names? And if you do, can you give them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milan Stanojevic was battalion commander. His deputy was Momir Pelemis. Assistant commander for intelligence and security was me. Assistant commander for morale and information was Private Dragan Pantic. The officer for general affairs was Private Rajko Babic. One of the drivers was Milan Jovanovic. The other was Milenko Pantic, I believe. The other two included Jovan Babic, who was the other Babic's assistant. And there was Zoran Markovic. Those are the two that I called operations officers. And maybe there were another two or three men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, if I can get the age of the witness, and if you ask the witness to describe what his task was as an assistant battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I guess -- could we go into private session for just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to your duties as assistant commander for security in July 1995, can you tell us what it is that you did, what your responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I worked inspecting the front line, touring the front line to size up the situation, and if I noticed any deficiencies and shortcomings, I would immediately, on that same day, report to the commander and his deputy so that they can take appropriate steps. As for intelligence work, we did very little, almost nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Vanderpuye, because we have noticed the witness getting a little bit fidgety with his headphones. Are they comfortable? Do you wish our usher to adjust them for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I feel like they're always falling off my head. That's why I keep touching them. I hear well, but they are not stable on my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see if that works better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed, and we will see. If they are not steady, then we will try to change them and get you another set.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, in terms of the security aspect -- the intelligence aspect of your position, you did very little, but could you tell us what it is you were supposed to do, what your responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I say "intelligence work," that means collecting data, collecting intelligence on the enemy around the front line. Since we did not have an intervention unit that was equipped for something like that, that is the reason why I said we did very little or next to nothing. The point was to tour the forward defence lines, the front lines, size up the situation and report to the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to 14th of July in 1995. Do you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you working on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was at the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As best as you can recall, can you tell us, did anything unusual happen that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember what you were doing in the morning of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Business as usual, like every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have contact with -- well, let me rephrase the question. Was the battalion commander present at the command on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the staff of the command was there except, I believe, the battalion commander. Maybe I should add that since I said earlier he was an indisputable authority, somebody no one dared to talk back at, there were quite a few problems in the operation of the battalion when he wasn't there. In normal times, the command worked in two shifts, in other words, it was divided into two groups. One was led by the commander, the other by the deputy. I was in the same shift as the battalion commander. In extraordinary situations like the period that we are going to discuss, the entire command would gather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the battalion commander was on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that a few days earlier, together with a group of 20 soldiers, he had gone to the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, who was in charge of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the battalion, it's only the commander and the deputy commander who have authority to issue orders. All the soldiers that I mentioned so far are on the same level as the soldiers on the frontline, except they did not do guard duty but had other duties that I spoke about earlier; to tour the defence lines and to report back to the commander about the shortcomings they had noticed. If you just give me one more minute, I can illustrate my case. For a while in 1995, we were digging trenches along the defence line. It was my job to make two trenches, together with two soldiers, and we finished that very soon. That evening, I sent one of the soldiers home to spend the night at home and come back to the front line the next day because he had worked very hard, and when I went back to the battalion command I said so to the commander. He immediately punished me by sending me to spend the night in the trench until the soldier comes back, just to show me who had the right to issue orders and make decisions and who doesn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. On the 14th, in particular, when the battalion commander was, as you recall, in Srebrenica or in that area, who was in charge of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The deputy commander, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with the deputy commander on the morning of the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During those days, he was upstairs in the same office as the battalion commander. The rest of us were on the ground floor of that house. And I'm not sure, but in the morning he came downstairs and told us he had talked to somebody at the brigade, and then he got more specific about what was going to follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as best as you can recall, what it is that he told you and the other men at the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said he had talked to somebody at the brigade and that person told him that a group of around 200 Muslim prisoners would be arriving and they would be put up in the schoolhouse near Kula. They would just spend the night there and be exchanged the next day somewhere. I believe a telegram followed soon after, and perhaps an hour after the telegram I spoke personally to Mr. Nikolic on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to your conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. Can he explain -- be specific which Nikolic he is referring to, please, for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "Mr. Nikolic," can you tell us who it is you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the news given us by the deputy commander and after the telegram received by the battalion command, perhaps an hour later I got a telephone call from Mr. Drago Nikolic, and he told me something very similar to what was written in the telegram. I believe he told me that it would be a good idea, regardless of who the deputy commander appoints to go down there, for me to be there as well to avoid any problems with the surrounding citizenry, because it is an inhabited area and my house is perhaps 100 metres from that school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we redact this last sentence, please? All right, leave it. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to get into the specifics of the conversation you had with Drago Nikolic, but first I just want to ask you: In terms of your -- in terms of what was related to you by the deputy battalion commander, did he indicate to you when it was these prisoners were expected at the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but on that day it was within a few hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about the number of individuals that would be assigned to go to this school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the number of 200 was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I perhaps did not phrase my question as accurately as I would have hoped, but when I mean the number of individuals that would be assigned, I'm talking about from the command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think anybody spoke about the number, because the battalion was facing a very difficult situation indeed. Its soldiers were scattered across four or five front lines. All the personnel was engaged. There was nobody who was free, and there was no available personnel, so I don't think a number was mentioned. It was just said that 10 or 15 people should be around the school when they arrive, and our main task was to avoid any disruption with the people who lived in the area, and that's what I discussed with Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. With respect to your conversation with Mr. Nikolic, can you -- do you recall specifically what he said? And? And if you do, can you relate that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have already said that. It is really necessary for me to repeat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask this question: In your previous answer to the question, you indicated that part of your conversation with Mr. Nikolic involved a consideration of the citizenry in the area. Can you recall specifically what was said about that, what you were expected to do or asked to do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try to summarise it in one sentence. He told me that it would be a good idea, regardless of who is appointed by deputy commander to go to the school, it would be a good idea for me to be there to avoid any problems with citizenry around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to that conversation, did you take that to be an order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Assistant commander for intelligence and security could not give me any orders. I have already described our relations at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have refused to go under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was nothing to refuse, because I didn't receive any orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the school following that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps an hour or two after that conversation, we finally set out to that school, to go to that school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time it's convenient for you, Mr. Vanderpuye, we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think now is perfect, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just at the break, sir, you indicated that you went to the school. Now, before you actually left to go to the school, did you discuss this conversation that you had with Drago Nikolic with the deputy commander of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible that I did tell him about this conversation that I had, but an hour before that we had received a telegram and he had already talked to somebody in the brigade. But I do think that I told him that I had this conversation with Drago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were among the -- were you among the people that were assigned to go to the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've already told you, our battalion had quite a lot of problems when the battalion commander was absent, and although there is no such thing as "we agreed" in the military, there was quite a lot of improvisation in our work. We often opted for makeshift solutions. So I can't really tell you that the battalion commander dispatched us to go there, but we just happened to receive this task and we, three or four of us from the battalion command, agreed that we would go there. We were actually quite taken aback by the task, but what I mean to say is even if the deputy commander had not sent me to go there, I would have gone there on my own initiative because my whole family was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so we're clear for the record, were you asked to go to the school by your deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will use the term "we agreed," the three or four of us, to go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this discussed in the presence of the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your presence among these other individuals or other people assigned to go to the school, was that influenced in any way by the conversation that you had with Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. You're trying to put it to me that Drago Nikolic had ordered me to go to the school. All the written documents that I received from Mr. Nikolic had, in the heading, something to the effect: "Information", "notice", so in those documents he merely pointed to certain issues that needed to be addressed. But all the documents originating from the brigade commander to the battalion had, in the heading or in the subject line, the words: "I order," or something to that effect. I'm really sorry that the commander was not there at the battalion headquarters, because he was the kind of man who would be able not to comply with the order from the brigade command. Had he been there and had we received the order to go to the school, it is quite possible that we would not have complied with this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Who went to the school with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I went there together with the general affairs clerk, Rajko Babic, and the assistant commander for morale and information, Dragan Pantic. I'm not sure whether or not a dozen or so soldiers went out together with us or whether they came later. I can't really be quite specific about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any arrangement to have other soldiers accompany you before you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before we left, I'm sure that no soldier had gone there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was whether any arrangement had been made at the command before you left to have a number of soldiers go to the school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've already explained, there were a lot of problems in the battalion, and we were quite taken aback when we received this telegram. The deputy commander himself didn't know what to do, but I think he managed to put together a group of maybe 10 or 15 men. I don't know how he did that. I think that they arrived at the school after the three of us arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time was it that you left the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't give you a definite answer, but it may have been around 12.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time did you arrive at the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the time frame. We may have headed out an hour or two later, and it may have taken us about an hour to get to the school. I don't know how we actually went there, but I cannot be specific about the time frame at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do when you got to the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got to the school, there was nobody there. I went to see my family to let them know that I had arrived, and I may have stayed there for some 20 minutes. As I went back towards the school, a convoy of vehicles had already been formed in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what you saw. What was this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were maybe some ten vehicles, most of them buses, and there may have been one or two trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see? Were there other soldiers, were there other people there when you came out from your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were some people there who had escorted those people. I didn't know them. By that time, they had already unloaded some of the prisoners and put them in the school gym. That was before I came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you arrived, what was the condition of the school? Was it open, was it closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was on my way back from my house, the gym was already full of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you first arrived, I mean, at the school, what was the condition of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "the condition."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it open or was it closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we didn't even get close to the door of the school building because we saw that there was nobody there, and then I just went on to my house. I guess it was locked, but that's just my guess, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came out, you saw the people were being put into the school. Do you have any idea how the school was opened for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you who opened the school because I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any preparations made to receive these prisoners by you or your men before they arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about that. While I was at home, I guess that Babic and Pantic remained there. But as to what they did, I can't tell you anything about that because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. About how many buses and trucks did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately a total of about ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many of these men that you didn't recognise did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, now you're asking me about details that I'm not sure I can give you an accurate answer. At the time when I got there, on my way back from the home, they had already pretty much filled the gym, and had it been possible to put all of them inside the gym, they would have unloaded all of them. And then we got into this conflict with them, and they stopped unloading people. But each vehicle had three to four men as escorts, so I can't give you an exact number of those people that I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the conflict that you had with these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you can properly call it a conflict. We asked them, "What are you doing?" And there was an exchange of harsh words, but regardless of what we said, they did what they wanted to do. And had it been possible for them to unload all of the prisoners there, I'm sure that they would have done so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this before or after the 10 or 15 people or men had been arranged -- that had been arranged by the deputy commander to go to the school arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that they actually arrived at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the 10 or 15 people that had been arranged by the commander, from what battalion were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were from the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they assigned to do once they arrived at the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our main task was to protect the local population, as I've already indicated. At no point in time were we able to exert any influence on the events that had to do with the unloading and treatment of those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the protection of the local population, what did those men do and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was a panic in the houses in the vicinity. I think that some families even took their family members to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I think that some 15 people, women, children, actually slept in my house in those days because they were afraid of what was happening in the school. At first, the people didn't even believe that something like that might happen, but when they saw what was going on, there was quite a lot of confusion there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything with respect to the local population before the prisoners actually arrived? Did you have any contact with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that everything happened very fast, but the few people that we spoke to didn't really believe what we said, and they had certain reservations about what we said. They simply didn't believe what we told them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, more or less that a group of prisoners would arrive and that they would spend the night there, that they would be there until the next morning, and that they shouldn't walk around, they shouldn't go there and watch, and so on. Things to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That occurred before you went to your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that, in passing, we may have spoken to two or three families. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The three of us from the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the soldiers that later arrived, what did they do with respect to this local population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were positioned at two or three points around the gym, and as to what their actual task was, it was to prevent any contact with the locals. There were quite a few curious people there who perhaps could even have gotten into the school building otherwise. There were many people in the immediate vicinity who had lost their closest kin. So all kinds of situations could have emerged. Those people may have been ready to do something, something worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the men were protecting the prisoners from the local population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the men also preventing the prisoners from escaping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's a complex issue, in fact. The sole authority over these people was exerted by the men who escorted them. They had the power to take them out at any point and do whatever they wished with them. We were there simply as silent observers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your men also preventing the prisoners from escaping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The prisoners never tried to escape at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that one of their tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that it's a complex situation. Tell us specifically what those men were tasked with when they arrived at the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, this question has been asked several times, and the witness has already answered it. We've kept quiet until now, but it really makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your objections are sustained. Move to your next question, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the men positioned around the school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic. One moment, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same objection again. The witness was asked this question and he answered by saying that there were two or three points, and so the answer is somewhere on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is whether he is asking the witness to identify the exact location of those three points. That far we can accept the question. Beyond that, obviously, you would be right, Ms. Nikolic. Or perhaps you can move straight to your next question, Mr. Vanderpuye. Let's come to the substance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, of the men -- well, what men were positioned around the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were no positions and nobody actually assigned those people to certain places. When our men came from the battalion, they stood around the school on their own initiative, and as I've already noted, we were completely taken aback by the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your men stood around the school where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has already answered this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I can respond to that, if you would allow me, but I don't think it would be appropriate to do it in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm of the opinion that you should move ahead, Mr. Vanderpuye. I think we've covered this. And then if, in the course of your next questions, it is important to refer the witness back to any exact location as regards him or any of his colleagues, you can do that. But let's move, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt one second, Mr. Vanderpuye? I meant to reserve this question until the last moment, but this is the third or fourth time the witness said that they had been taken aback. Witness, you said that you and others were taken aback when you were informed that the prisoners were to be arriving at Pilica School. Can I ask the reason why you were taken aback?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, the troops in our battalion were mostly -- well, 99 per cent of them were just villagers, and they held a line in front of our village and they had absolutely no war experience, no combat experience. In the four years of war, none of us had ever seen this enemy of ours in the flesh, and the thing that was about to happen at the school was -- came as a great surprise to all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the thing that was about to happen at the school"? They were just prisoners, and as you indicate, they never tried to escape. If they were detained or later exchanged, what problem would there have been? My question is whether you were aware at the moment they were to be executed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely, and we did not become aware for quite a long time of what would happen. But their arrival in our village was something that caused a great deal of concern for us, us in the battalion, but this was an event that we had no influence over, right from the start up until the very -- up until the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you further elaborate why that was a concern to your battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation in the battalion was quite complex. The line was weak. There were just one or two men manning the trenches. And on top of all those problems that we had, now we had those prisoners to think about and to worry about, and the battalion commander was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And please remember our suggestion to move forward, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was just going to follow up on some of the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You're free to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What specifically were you worried about with respect to these prisoners in the town?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is precisely the -- as I understand it, unless I'm becoming deficient, that's the answer that -- the question that Judge Kwon put and the witness answered. Correct me if I am not understanding well, please I stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't wish to correct you, Mr. President, but the answer was: "It was a complex situation and that there were problems and we had to think about them and worry about them." And that doesn't answer the question, which is why I put it to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's explained. The panic that was created amongst the population, the lack of combat preparedness, preparation, on the part of his group, the absence of the commander, and do I have to continue and finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll just take it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move. Okay, let's move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with these soldiers that you said you didn't recognise during the time that you were at the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ascertain who was commanding these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to ascertain who was commanding these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They ruled the overall situation. I suppose they had contact with their superior, and we were on the sideline all the time. Maybe we did have superficial contact with them, but it was nothing that could significantly influence the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ascertain from them what was to be done with these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think from the very start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness was asked whether he had contact with these soldiers. His answer was, "No." What is the basis for this follow-up question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He also said that there may have been some contact. He did not exclude it categorically. So I would rephrase your question and put to the witness whether at least they asked these soldiers how long these prisoners were going to be kept, how long the situation was going to persist, what was going to happen. Perhaps you can direct your question along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I just didn't want to lead the witness in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless I hear an objection, you are being given the go-ahead to lead in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out from these prisoners -- from these soldiers how long these prisoners were to stay at this school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that from the very start, we found out, although I don't know how, that they would just spend the night there, and the next morning would be exchanged. How we got that information, I don't know, but everybody who was there knew it. It's even possible that from the moment we left the battalion command, we had that information, but I cannot be sure about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody from the command that you were with at this school have contact with these soldiers that you didn't recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose there were individual contacts, one to one, but the event proceeded according to the instructions of the people who came in escort of these prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they give you particular instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't need to contact with us at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what the condition of the school or the condition of the prisoners were while you were at the school on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went into the school just once or twice over those two days. Rajko Babic spent more time inside. Therefore, I cannot say much about the condition of the prisoners. I just glanced inside the gym once or twice from the doorway. A very unpleasant smell emanated from there, and you couldn't bear to be in the doorway for more than a minute or two. When the guard who was inside went out, they would shift and cover the entire floor. And when the guard would come in to tell them something, they would suddenly withdraw and only occupy one-third of the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guard that you're speaking about, was that a member of your battalion or was that someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm speaking all the time about those men who came in their escort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you went inside the school, did you do that under some direction or instruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only went in to see what the situation was like. There was no one there who could give me any orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report what you observed to your deputy commander, or the deputy commander of the battalion, to be more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we spoke more than once over that period while they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you tell in relation to the condition of the prisoners and the security situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we spoke for the first time on the 15th in the morning. That is when we realised that those people were not leaving, as we had been told earlier. I think that's when he called me and told me that he had spoken with someone from the brigade command. He had requested that those people be driven away from somewhere else, but this request was not met with any understanding. That's when we agreed between us that I, too, should go to the brigade command for the same purpose, to demand from somebody that those people be driven somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any discussion with him concerning the objection that you had that had taken place earlier on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible that we exchanged a couple of sentences concerning what was going on around the school. But I repeat this. There were men who were in control of that situation. We had no influence on that. Our only desire was that those people be driven somewhere else as soon as possible. That's why he approached the superior command with that request, and that's why I was going there, for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the prisoners that were not in the school, can you tell us where they were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, those five or so vehicles that had not been unloaded remained standing outside the school, and I think they spent the night there, the night of the 14th. On the morning of the 15th, and I'm not sure about the time, I suppose that they had spoken to somebody in the meantime. In any case, the vehicles turned around and left away from the village. We didn't know where they were going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how those vehicles were secured, if at all, during that night, the night of the 14th, into the 15th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were guarded by those people who were in escort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the morning of the -- let me withdraw that. Where did you spend the night, that is, the night of the 14th, into the 15th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night, maybe until midnight, I was with troops, and then around midnight, perhaps, I went home to get some rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in contact with the other members of the command after you left to go home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we said hello and goodbye to each other. It was a matter of course that I was going to tell them that I was going home. Babic, Pantic and I were not there all the time. We took turns, and each of us was there only half of the time. But exactly how long our stints were, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps it was a translation misunderstanding, but my question is: After you went home, were you in contact with these other members of the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was it that you -- when was it that you resumed contact with them on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when I arrived that morning. Maybe around 6.00. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would appreciate it if my learned friend would specify which command he is asking about. The battalion command or the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's well taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure Mr. Vanderpuye will oblige.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the battalion command, the members who actually went with you to the school. Those are the command members I'm talking about. I think -- well, you tell me. Your answer, did you understand it when I put it to you, the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understood. I meant members of the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in around 6.00 in the morning, what was the nature of that contact? Were you provided with any information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the next contact we had when I came back to the school, maybe we exchanged a few words like were there any problems in the meantime and such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information that there had been any problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They told me there had been no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information there had been any incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive any information as to the condition of the prisoners overnight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was only concerned and talked about our soldiers, not prisoners, but we were able to note that the night had passed and we were waiting to see what was going to happen from the morning of the 15th on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I've already mentioned that conversation between me and the deputy, the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do after that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After he told me he had spoken to someone himself, we agreed that I was going to go to the brigade command myself, and I think it was about 10.00 or 11.00 that I left, together with a driver, Milan Jovanovic, for the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go straight to the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go once you reached the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to see the commanding officer on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly who it was, but there were four or five commanding officers from the brigade there talking about the chaotic situation, and it was a laden atmosphere. They barely noticed me when I came in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we proceed any further, just two points that need to be established. One is: He and the other members of his group that went to Kula School, whether they were wearing uniforms, and, secondly, whether they were carrying any weapons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you've understood the President's question. When you went with the other members of the command to the school, were you armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that Pantic, Babic and I did not have weapons, while the soldiers did have their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they arrive there in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot be sure. There was some men who didn't have a uniform at all, and they manned the front lines in their regular clothes. So I cannot emphatically claim that everybody was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the other members of the command that were with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were in uniform, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the individuals that you didn't -- or the people that you didn't recognise there, the soldiers, were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think they were in military uniform too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniforms they were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I can be precise, and I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the command, did you have a discussion with anybody about the circumstances concerning the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I had an informal discussion starting with those four or five commanding officers, and I was trying to paint the situation in even more dramatic terms that it actually was. I think I even said that two of the prisoners had escaped. They first bought this story, but then I admitted very soon that it wasn't actually true. I was simply taken aback by the lack of concern they displayed about the problem I came to discuss with them. I gave it a lot of thought, and I think it's not normal, when somebody from a battalion command comes to see the brigade command, and they are treated in that way. I told them immediately why I was there, but they seemed totally preoccupied with the situation about capturing some line or other. They were talking about the losses our side had sustained. But I came away from all that with a conclusion that it was possible that even this operation, I mean the school, was controlled from a level much higher than that of the brigade even, and I came away with that impression because my arrival and what I said to them barely registered with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's not an objection. It's just a question of interpretation. It's page 52, line 5, where it says "commanding officers," "five commanding officers." It has a different connotation than what the witness said. The witness said "officers from the command." Maybe it should be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the word used by the witness is "staresina", and that is, as we were told, translated by commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank Ms. Nikolic and I also thank the interpreter for letting us know the exact word, Serbian word, used by the witness. As I recall, the witness earlier on referred to four or five duty officers or officers on duty at the -- from the brigade at the command building, so I think we need to know whether we are still referring to the same persons, first of all, and which would be the best description to fit the role that they had at the time. I think the witness himself can help us here. I mean, these four or five or six persons that you tried to convince, who were they exactly? I'm not asking you for the names because you've already said that you don't know any names, but what was their office at the time, what was their rank, or what were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were commanding officers from the brigade, but what exactly each of their job was, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were they together or did you speak to them separately, or how come that you met not just with one commanding officer but with four or five at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an office where the duty officer usually sits, the duty officer for the brigade. But at that moment inside that office, there were four or five commanding officers who were discussing something, namely, the thing that I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness, what you mean by "commanding officer," an officer in the position of a commander? For example, company commander or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Company level does not exist in the brigade. It exists only in the battalion. So these officers were employed in the brigade command, but what exactly each of them was responsible for, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what specifically was the response that you received to your request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I've already mentioned it. They seemed totally uninterested in what I was saying, and that's why I drew the conclusions I drew. But one of them, I think, asked me, "Are there any woods close to where you are," something like that, like, "Why aren't you killing them off?" I said that I and my men cannot kill a single person, and I think one of them responded something like, "If you are not going to kill them, then let them drown you all down at the village."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we move, you're still not in a position to tell us who this person was, this commanding officer who spoke to you in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really don't remember who those officers were. I think that one of the four or five may have been Captain Jokic, but I'm not sure who was actually engaged in this conversation that I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, specifically what did you request from these officers that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only request that I made was for them to drive them away from the Kula School as soon as possible, and my impression was that they, themselves, had no influence over the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask any of these officers to convey your request to the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that one of them left the office and came back quite soon, and he said that Major Obrenovic -- whether he had actually seen him or spoken to him, I don't know, but what he relayed to us was that there was a total lack of interest in that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What you've just told us, in other words, one of these commanding officers coming back to you mentioning Major Obrenovic, possibly, and the rest, was this after or before that one of the commanding officers had spoken to you about woods around Pilica and killing of prisoners? Was it before or after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try as I might, I cannot establish a time-line of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One further question. When you first arrived at the post, there were these commanding officers in the room of the duty officer. How could you establish that the four or five of them were all commanding officers? Did they tell you so or did they have any insignia that could explain this to you? How did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know most of the officers in the Zvornik Brigade, so I knew them by sight, I knew their faces, and that is how I was able to tell that there was nobody from the outside there, because I went to the brigade command quite often. I think that there was a very small number of people there that I wasn't able to recognise by sight. In other words, I knew what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person that told you -- this officer that told you that you should kill these prisoners, did he attribute that statement or remark to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't speak about that with any degree of certainty. It is possible that he may have invoked Major Obrenovic as an authority, but I cannot be definite about it. So this was an informal conversation between me and them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt a minute here? I noted it. Page 55, line 13 to 15, he said he stopped -- he said that Major Obrenovic did something, but I didn't hear he said anything about Major Obrenovic. Could you clarify with the witness further? So I wonder whether there is a total lack of interest in that problem is a description of what Major Obrenovic responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had indicated, in response to a question I asked about, what specifically you requested from these officers. In your answer, you said that the person came back and said that Major Obrenovic -- and then you stopped, and then you indicated that that person relayed that there was a total lack of interest in the problem. The question is: Is that -- was the person relaying to you what Major Obrenovic was saying about the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This gentleman that went out came back after a brief period of time, and he invoked his authority. Now, I don't know whether he saw him or merely spoke to him.
