I can only speculate on that. But what he relayed to me is that there was a complete lack of interest in the problem, which was abnormal, it was unusual. We have a situation as follows: I come to the brigade's command and I ask these people to be taken away, and the least that they should have told me was we would come in an hour or somebody would come in an hour or two, a day or two. Based on the fact that nobody gave me any response, I concluded, and that's my personal conclusion, that this operation had been conducted from a level that was way higher than that of a brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at page 57, my learned colleague asked the witness -- I'm sorry, 56, line 15, I will now read in English because I cannot translate: [In English] "This person that told you, this officer that told you, that you should kill these prisoners." [Interpretation] The witness never said that this officer had said something to that effect, because if we look at lines 17 through 20 of page 57 -- 54, we can see that what the witness said is completely different from this suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, point taken. The rest can become a submission, but point taken, Ms. Nikolic. I think we can safely proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just catching up with you. I want to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, the witness had said, if you look at page 54, line 19: "But one of them, I think, asked me, 'Are there any woods close to where you are,' something like that, like, 'Why aren't you killing them off?' I said that I and my men and I cannot kill a single person. And I think one of them responded something like, 'If you are not going to kill them, then let them drown you all down at the village." It's Ms. Nikolic's position that this cannot be condensed in the words that you used when you put one of the questions, one of the subsequent questions to the witness, page 56, line 15 and 16: "This person that told you -- that told you that you should kill these prisoners, did he attribute that statement to him or anyone else." This is basically -- there is disagreement between your way of putting it and her way of understanding the words of the witness, this is it. I'm obviously not commenting on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think as I said before, it's time we proceed, basically. We've taken the point made by Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after you had this discussion at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, I went back to the village, and I was a much more worried man than I had been when I had left, because at that point in time I suddenly began to realise the seriousness of the situation we were in. As first, we had been told that these people would spend there just one night and that they would be taken away the next morning. I went to the brigade command and I got no answer there. And when I got to the school, my men expected me to tell them what the results of my visits were, and I think that there was no need for them to ask any questions. All they had to do was look at me and they knew more or less what the result was. I was angry, in a foul mood, and that meant that there was no light at the end of this tunnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stop anywhere on the way back to the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Since in the meantime we had heard that there were some prisoners in the Pilica culture hall, the dom, I went to the village centre with the driver, and across the road from the culture hall, and they may have spent there a minute or two. I merely wanted to have a look at what was going on down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I was able to see was that there was security around this area, and those were again men I didn't know. There was no need for me to get any closer because there were no soldiers from our battalion there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these men in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there were military uniforms and police uniforms too. That's what I was able to see from a distance of maybe 50 or 60 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there vehicles, military vehicles, in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, but I can't really be very specific about this and give you too many details, because I spent a very short time there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me if you've already answered this, but how long did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, you went to the school. Did you go directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you communicate your observations of the dom to the deputy commander of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do when you got back to the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing specific. The second day was slowly coming to a close, and we were beginning to realise that we would spend another night there too. I probably spoke to the deputy commander and relayed to him the results of my visits to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did the deputy commander do or say as a result of what you told him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All we could do was to express our concern about the future course of events, and in one of the conversations I think that we agreed that we have to rotate the 15 or so soldiers that were stationed there and replace them by other soldiers. And I think that in the evening of the 15th, he sent 15 soldiers, and the 15 soldiers who had been there at the school went -- either they went home or they went to the lines. I can't be more specific. So the second night passed. I was again there perhaps until 2200 hours, and then I went home to rest until the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the second night, you mean the night of the 15th, into the 16th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went home, were you in contact with other members of the battalion command who had accompanied you there in the first instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "contact."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in radio contact with them or telephone contact with them once you left the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about in contact with the deputy commander of the battalion; were you in contact with him overnight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not during the night. I did have, I think, a Motorola with me, and we spoke throughout the day maybe two or three times over that Motorola. But when I got home for the night, I did not have any contact either with the deputy commander or the people that had remained there at the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the time that you came back to the school from the dom and the time you went home, how much time did you actually spend at the school itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say. I'd often leave during the day, so perhaps I spent half of the time there and half of the time I was somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were there, did you become aware of any problems relating to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not. Usually when I got back, I talked to Babic or Pantic and I'd ask them if there had been any problems, and they would tell me that there had been no incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your recollection of what you were told on the 15th and 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness replied quite clearly that this was the 16th or, rather, that it wasn't the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The confusion may be with respect to the translation, because the answer says, "That's what they would tell me," and that suggests that he's talking about more than one instance. And that's the reason why the question was put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's the case of going ahead. You need to repeat your question now, I think, because I want to make sure that it goes clear, reaches the witness in a clear manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Is your recollection of what you were told on the 15th by Babic or Pantic that there had been no incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the same recollection with respect to what you were told by Babic or Pantic on the morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were at the school on the 15th, did you yourself become aware of any incidents involving the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our main interest, what we wanted to do most of all, was to get those prisoners out of there as soon as possible. As for the treatment afforded those prisoners, this is something that was up to the people who were escorting them, but I was not present when there were any incidents on the parts that involved the soldiers who were escorting them, so they did not mistreat or abuse in any way those prisoners. They treated them in a -- like military men, but there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the morning of the 16th, after you spoke with Babic or Pantic, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at around 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning, I was called by the deputy commander, and he told me more or less the following: That somebody from the brigade command had called him and that he had been told that we should not worry, that people would finally come and take those prisoners away from there. And we were greatly relieved to hear that, all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say where these prisoners were going to be taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say when they were going to be removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really say, but he may have said something about in two or three hours, somebody would come in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he say how they were going to be removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. He merely said that I should not worry, that some people would come and take them away, and he did not go beyond that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What happened after that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we waited for somebody to come to take those people away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did somebody come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think at around 1200 hours, two officers came. I didn't know them. That was the first and the last time I saw them. And then a van came. There may have been about a dozen soldiers in that van. And then an empty bus came.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I think this is a good spot to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where we left off, you'd indicated that around 1200 hours on the 16th, two officers came. Before these officers arrived, did you see any bodies in and around the area of the school, the road, in that vicinity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports about any bodies in the vicinity of the school or that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any bodies on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the 14th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive any reports about bodies on the 15th or the 14th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, really not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when these officers arrived, tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already said. After they arrived, a van came carrying ten soldiers or so, and the van was followed by an empty bus. They were rather insolent and arrogant towards us, and they immediately started loading and taking away the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they were insolent and arrogant, can you just describe for us what you saw them do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which word to use, but they were rather hostile towards us from the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. For what reason, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The van that you saw, could you describe what colour it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, really, those are details I can't speak about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you see these officers actually do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that as soon as they arrived, the operation of loading and taking away the prisoners started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see them interacting with anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm really not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any interaction with them, personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not me, personally, but one of our soldiers told me that one of them had asked after me. He wanted to know where I was. I wasn't there at the moment. And I think that person said that I was going to the brigade to complain. They didn't need to talk to anybody. They probably had a very clear purpose, a clear objective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the soldier tell you which one of the two had asked after you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask the soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It didn't matter to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe these two officers that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One of them was very tall, going bald, with striking features. I think the other one was a bit shorter than the first, dark-haired, but I remember the first one more clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall giving a description of these two officers previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're driving at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall having described these two officers on a prior occasion before today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible that I described them in the same way I did now. That was the only time I ever saw those people. To the best of my recollection, that's what they looked like, but who they are, I really cannot say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Do you recall having given a description of them on a prior occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this has been asked and answered. He just asked it and the witness said, "It's possible that I did," so is he just going to keep asking this question repeatedly, because he's answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would beg to differ with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I beg to differ with my colleague. What was -- the witness said it's possible that he described them in the way he did previously. My question is whether or not he recalls having described them. That's a "yes" or "no" -- that's a "yes" or "no" question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The previous question was: "Do you recall having described these two officers on a prior occasion before today?" Which is exactly the same question which you're putting now. His answer was: "It's possible I described them in the same way I did now. That was the only time I ever saw these people. To the best of my recollection, that's what they looked like, but who they are, I really cannot say with any certainty." Now, the question is: "Do you recall having given a description of them on a prior occasion?" So the two are different. I mean, the previous one was: "Do you recall having ever described on a previous occasion," and now it refers directly to a possible description that he may have given before. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go straight to the point. You can try to refresh the witness's memory, if you are in a position to do so, and then we'll see what he has to say. But the two questions are, although they look the same, they are actually somewhat different, and one follows the previous one. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember describing these individuals as one being quite strongly built, quite bulky, with grey hair, and the other being quite shorter, wearing a moustache, with a dark complexion? Do you recall having given that description of these officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am testifying here under oath, and I don't want to say anything rash. I saw those men then for the first and the last time in my life. I really don't know who they were. And this description that you included in your question, I believe, is not in dispute. I think I have explained what they both looked like, and that's all I can say. I am sure that they were not commanding officers from the Zvornik Brigade, because as I said before, I know most of the officers of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it accurate, therefore, that the shorter of the two had dark hair and a moustache?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've said he was dark-haired, dark-eyed. I said in my statement that he had a moustache, but I am not absolutely certain about that. I remember the first one well. You insist that he had a moustache. I know that I said that in one of my statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to the taller one, is it fair to say that you previously described him as being quite strongly built, quite bulky, with grey hair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've said several times that was the first and the last time that you saw these officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any subsequent time see them either in photos or in the press?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, first, do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you believe those officers to be, after having seen photos in the press?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't understand the gist of your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever reach a conclusion as to who these officers were that you -- who they were that you saw on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, approximately, they bore some similarity to those men that I described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were those people that you saw in the press? What were their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, really, I wouldn't like to name anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if you've previously named anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I named Beara and Popovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as what you observed on the 16th, were those officers present at the time that the prisoners were taken out of the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were -- they bore some resemblance to those people, but whether it was them, I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you hear the -- the shorter of the two, did you hear him being referred to by any name in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think one of his soldiers called him by a shortened version of a name, "Pope," P-o-p-e.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you certain that's what you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was that individual present at the time that these prisoners were removed from the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot be precise about the sequence of events now. I said as soon as they arrived, they started loading and driving the prisoners away. Where each one of them was at any given moment, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe the prisoners being removed from the school, yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was at a distance of perhaps 50 metres, and we all watched what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Am I given to understand that you never actually saw the prisoners being removed from the school, by your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. All of us who were there saw them load the prisoners in and drive them away, but what I cannot say is where everyone was positioned at that moment. Certainly, I saw the bus being loaded and driving away. I don't know what exactly you're insisting on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the prisoners -- were their hands bound, were they blindfolded? Can you tell us what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be sure about the hands, but as the bus was passing by us, I believe I saw them blindfolded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time that you observed the bus leave, did you have any indication as to where it was going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm sure that none of us present there knew at that moment what was going to happen to those people. But when the second and the third bus departed, you could hear at a distance some shots, and I suppose we thought that one of the possibilities was that they were taking them not very far away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the prisoners on the bus, were they secured in some way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The prisoners on the bus who were there on the 14th, at night, left on the morning of the 15th. I don't know exactly what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's my fault. I'm talking about the prisoners on the bus on the 16th that you observed from about 50 metres away. Were they secured in some way by soldiers or some other unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe they were followed by those soldiers who had guarded them at the school and who had come with them in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've indicated that they were taking them not very far away and you heard shots, and what did you understand to be going on at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one of the possibilities was that we assumed that somewhere not far away, an execution was being carried out, judging by the shots we heard, but we were not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say how many buses were involved in this operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think one bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about how long did this operation continue, or last, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps for about two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that -- during that period of time, were you in contact with the deputy battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think the first time I saw him again was soon after that, when we returned to the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were the soldiers from the 1st Battalion while this was being carried out, generally? I'm not asking you specifically soldier by soldier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, approximately, as I described the first time, somewhere outside, and I was probably with them at that moment. That means that they were not at all involved in the loading, escorting and execution of these prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you can -- you can safely account for all of the soldiers that were at the school on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, none of those people who came required anything of us. They acted on their own instructions. I cannot be 100 per cent sure that none of our soldiers boarded the bus at some point out of curiosity. To the best of my knowledge, they didn't, but, how shall I put it, I can't be 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Just bear with me for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the two officers that you saw accompany the bus out of the school during the period of time this operation was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, but those are details that I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you present when they left, if at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not present there all the time while they were driving the prisoners away, but I believe that they were there until the end, and then they left in one direction and we, people from my battalion and I, left in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They left together, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Really, although I'm trying very hard, I cannot remember these details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I have -- if you could just approximate for us, about how many people were in the school or removed from the school and driven away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for the bus to get from the school to the place where the execution was carried out, it took it about two hours to go there and back, so there must have been about four or five buses, at the most, judging by the length of the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "four or five buses," do you mean four or five trips or do you mean literally that there were four or five buses that came on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was one bus, so a total of four or five bus-fulls of prisoners were driven there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I have no further questions at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. We've got 20 minutes before we adjourn. I have on my list almost all the Defence teams wishing to cross-examine this witness except for the Gvero Defence team. Who wishes to go first? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Witness, the first time that you spoke about these events was in 2003, is that right? When you gave those interviews to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I spoke to them twice. The first time was on the 5th and the second was on the 10th of March, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the events that you testified about today, at that time almost eight years had passed from those events, so my first question to you is: How well were you able to recall those events at the time when you gave those interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, believe me, even today when I discuss those things with some people, I have some doubts about the exact way those events occurred. A long time has passed, and I can never agree to what other people say about some events that were in the past. I always talk about these things the way I recall them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, you've had the opportunity, from the time of the events until the time that you gave the interview, to hear a lot about those events from media reports and from other people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, this event is not discussed all that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to read about it in the papers or to follow the news coverage on TV, things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the Srebrenica events are always a hot topic, and that's -- that is so even in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You must have heard that judgements have been passed regarding those events, and you probably were able to hear what was adjudicated, what was stated in the judgements. I'm not trying to say that you read the judgements themselves, but that you followed the reports in the media.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite specifically, there were a couple of Srebrenica trials before this Tribunal, the Krstic trial, the Blagojevic and Jokic trial, and there were some other trials that ended with the guilty plea, Erdemovic, Obrenovic, Momir Nikolic and so on, and the media reported quite extensively on all those events. Were you able to read anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, I read the papers quite regularly, and so I do have some knowledge about those events, and I'm aware of the latest judgement before another court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, did those reports or this information in any way influence your thoughts or your efforts to remember the events that you witnessed on the 16th of July in front of the Pilica school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not -- I'm not sure what you're driving at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one usually gathers information from different sources. You hear something, you see something, and you hear something indirectly or you read about it, and I think that after a while all this information merges, and after a while one is no longer sure what one has actually seen or heard or what one has only read about. There is an amalgam of all those different reports after a while and you can't remember the exact source of some knowledge that you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time -- I apologise. I think that there has been a misinterpretation. I think that what the witness said is that there is this possibility, and it appears that the interpreter's answer is different from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me put the question straight to him, because basically this is what you're trying to elicit from the witness. Mr. Zivanovic has referred you to your statements on the events in Kula and way back in July of 1995. The question is: Have you recounted these events based on your conviction of what you saw and lived during those days or has your description of the events been influenced by what you may have read or seen in the media following the Srebrenica cases before this Tribunal? I've tried to condense Mr. Zivanovic's question as best as I could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for the most part, I gave my answers on the basis of what I saw. And now as to the actual percentage of the effects of the media reports that were to follow after those events, I can't really be very specific about it. I can't tell you to what extent this influenced me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has it influenced you to the extent of you having given us information or stated -- made statements here that are not based on your own knowledge of the events? In other words, are you basing yourself or giving us facts which are not based on what you lived through but based on what you heard in these cases, in which case you need to tell us which.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to be more precise in my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am convinced that you did not consciously say -- state here that you saw something, when in fact you didn't see something. I simply asked you whether it is possible that what you heard or had seen on TV or heard from some other sources somehow got merged with what you personally saw, and in particular with what you were able to see for a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would very much like to be able to answer some more specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me be quite specific, then. You gave us a description of a person that you said was an officer who showed up in front of the Pilica school on the 16th of July, 1995, and on that occasion you said that this was a man who was shorter than the other person. You said that the person had dark hair. This is what you stated today. And you were not sure whether this person had or did not have a moustache. When the Prosecutor asked you whether, in your interview, you spoke about a moustache, you said that you did. Now, what I want to know is the following: How accurate is your recollection, in the first place, that this person had or did not have a moustache?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know what to tell you. I'm now giving evidence 12 years after the event. This is an extremely long time period. What I recall about the appearance of these people is what I told you. I cannot add or take away anything. In my statement, I did state that this person had a moustache, but I cannot be a million per cent sure. And I said that I was more certain that I could better recall the appearance of the first man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are we to understand this to mean that you are not sure that this person had a moustache or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you can phrase it any way you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like you to phrase it to give me an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave you my answer. In my statement, the 2003 statement, I said that he had a moustache, but now I cannot state with a million per cent certainty that this was indeed so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's one more thing that I'm interested in when we're dealing with this topic. You also stated that you had seen pictures of some of those people, and what I want to know is whether those pictures may have affected your -- the image in your head that you had when you gave the interview regarding the question of whether this person had or did not have a moustache?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to move on to a different question. You said that the soldiers addressed one of these men as "Pope" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you move to this question, Witness, these photos that you have mentioned before and to which Mr. Zivanovic has referred you, where did you see them? Did you see them before you came here to give -- before you were interrogated or interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor or did you see them while you were being interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was before the interview with the Prosecution. I don't know when this whole thing became so topical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in the course of the interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, were you shown photos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to go on with my question. Would you agree with me that this nickname Pop or Pope, that this in fact is a nickname in our language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it can also be a designation of a profession, because this is the word used to address priests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, it can have a number of meanings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were a rank-and-file soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995. Could you please tell me, when you wanted to address an active-duty officer, for instance, a lieutenant-colonel, did you have to address him as "Lieutenant-Colonel, sir"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not only lieutenant-colonels but even junior officers had to be addressed in the usual way, dictated by the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you complied with the rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the other soldiers? As far as you know, did they also comply with those rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have any lieutenant-colonels. I've already said that apart from some of the officers in the brigade command, all the others were just soldiers, privates, and they were there as battalion commanders and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I merely use this rank, lieutenant-colonel, as an example, but I merely wanted to ask you whether all the troops, privates, had to address officers in the way that I just explained to you, in other words, using the term "sir" and the rank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I already noted, even junior officers were treated with respect and addressed in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: If you, as a rank-and-file soldier, as a private, talked to -- wanted to address another soldier, did you use the informal way of addressing, in other words, names, nicknames?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it would depend. In some cases, you would use a name, in other cases you would use a nickname. It would depend on the actual circumstances. It would depend on the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, a private did not address a private using the words "sir" or "private"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But it was quite usual, in other words, to use the person's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Or a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it would depend on the relationship they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two minutes left. It's up to you. If you are embarking on a new -- and you can finish it in two minutes, go ahead. If not, we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just one question, and then we can continue the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you hear a soldier, a private, use a nickname as a form of address, if he says "Pope," would that indicate to you that this soldier was addressing an assistant commander of the corps, an assistant corps commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this would be an appropriate moment to stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Witness, we need to stop here because our time is over. You will return here on Monday morning at 9.00 p.m. [sic] to continue -- 9.00 a.m. to continue and hopefully finish your testimony. Between now and Monday, you are not to communicate with anyone or let anyone try to discuss with you the substance of your testimony, that is, the events that you are testifying upon. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a nice weekend, everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of May, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 25
